subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 34-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back; serum triglycerides are 3800 mg/dL, and the serum specimen shows a creamy supernatant layer. He has had two previous episodes of pancreatitis and has eruptive xanthomas over the buttocks. LDL and HDL cholesterol are normal or low, and fasting chylomicron levels are markedly elevated.
question: A defect in which of the following apolipoproteins is the most likely cause of his disorder?
explanation_correct: Familial hyperchylomicronemia (type I dyslipidemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder most often caused by deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or of its activating cofactor, apo CII. Without functional apo CII, chylomicron triglycerides are not hydrolyzed, producing massive hypertriglyceridemia, a creamy supernatant, eruptive xanthomas, and recurrent pancreatitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Apo A-I is the major structural protein of HDL and activates LCAT; its deficiency lowers HDL but does not cause chylomicronemia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Apo B48 is required for chylomicron secretion from enterocytes; defective apo B48 assembly, as in abetalipoproteinemia, causes fat malabsorption rather than chylomicronemia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Apo B100 binds the LDL receptor, and its defect (familial hypercholesterolemia type II) raises LDL cholesterol rather than chylomicrons.
explanation_incorrect.E: Apo E mediates hepatic uptake of chylomicron remnants and IDL; its defect (type III dysbetalipoproteinemia) causes mixed hyperlipidemia with palmar xanthomas, not isolated chylomicronemia.

educationalObjective: Apo CII activates lipoprotein lipase, so its deficiency causes familial hyperchylomicronemia with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas.
